selected_lines.text: # Exit codes
This page is the exit-code contract of `mcpmoat scan`. Other docs give a short form and link
here.
| Code | Meaning |
| 0 | No execution error, and no finding that is not ignored has severity at or above `--fail-on`. |
| 1 | No execution error, and at least one finding that is not ignored has severity at or above `--fail-on`. |
| 2 | Execution or usage error. Exit code 2 wins over 1. |
- `--fail-on low|medium|high|critical` sets the lowest severity that gives exit code 1. The default
is `high`. Only these exact lowercase words work. Another value, an empty value or a second
`--fail-on` is a usage error (exit code 2). It is a `scan` flag only. `pin` never exits with
code 1.
- Ignored findings (`--ignore`, or `.mcpmoat-ignore` with `--use-ignore-file`) never give exit
code 1. Without `--use-ignore-file`, `scan` does not read the file, so it drops nothing (see
[Ignore findings](ignore.md)).
- With `--llm`, the LLM findings (`MOAT-LLM-001`, `MOAT-LLM-002`) count like any other finding.
They are `high` at most.
- mcpmoat fails closed. A finding with a severity that mcpmoat does not know always counts, at
every `--fail-on` value. A finding whose rule ID is not in the rule set counts as critical.
- No built-in rule is critical yet, so `--fail-on critical` passes every built-in finding, also a
rug pull (`MOAT-T2-001` is high). `scan` says so on stderr: `mcpmoat scan: note: no built-in
rule is critical yet, so with --fail-on critical no built-in finding gives exit code 1`. It fails
only in the two fail-closed cases above, or when a description or schema rule from `--rules` is
critical: then a finding of that rule and a `MOAT-T1-023` budget finding or a `MOAT-T1-024` cap
finding (see below) give exit code 1.
- An unpinned server that fails or times out is a warning only (in the summary, or on stderr with
`--json`). It does not change the exit code. A pinned server that fails or times out is a high
`MOAT-T2-004` finding.
- The rule analysis shares one time limit between all servers (see [Limits](limits.md)). A server
that uses up its share is a `MOAT-T1-023` finding. A server that `scan` does not reach in time
is not analysed, and the servers after it are not analysed either. Each of them gets the same
finding for all its tools. Its severity is the highest severity
of the description and schema rules that `scan` applies, but never lower than high. So it is
high with the built-in rules, and critical when a description or schema rule from `--rules` is
critical (see the `--fail-on critical` item above). It is not an execution error: it gives exit
code 1 with the default `--fail-on`, and the JSON `complete` stays `true`. Only a signal (see
below) stops the scan with exit code 2; the end of the time limit does not. `scan` also prints a
warning on stderr (see [Scan output](scan-output.md)). A `.mcpmoat-ignore` file cannot drop the
finding. Only `--ignore MOAT-T1-023` can.
- `scan` lists at most 1000 tool rule findings for each server, the most severe ones. It counts the
rest and adds one `MOAT-T1-024` finding that says how many it left out ("N more tool findings are
not listed; limit M"). Its severity is the highest severity of the description and schema rules that `scan`
applies, but never lower than high, as for `MOAT-T1-023`. It is not an execution error: it gives
exit code 1 with the default `--fail-on`, and the JSON `complete` stays `true`. The exit code
follows `--fail-on` like for any other finding. A `.mcpmoat-ignore` file cannot drop it, also
with `--use-ignore-file`, because it can come from a cloned repository. Only
`--ignore MOAT-T1-024` can.
- `scan` lists at most 100 config findings (`MOAT-T4-*` and `MOAT-T5-*`) for each server and
10,000 for the whole scan, the most severe ones. A server that loses config findings to a limit
gets one `MOAT-T4-005` finding that says how many it left out ("N more config findings are not
listed; limit M"). Its severity is high, or higher when a finding that it left out is higher. It
is not an execution error: it gives exit code 1 with the default `--fail-on`, and the JSON
`complete` stays `true`. A `.mcpmoat-ignore` file cannot drop it. Only `--ignore MOAT-T4-005`
can (see [Limits](limits.md)).
Exit code 2 comes, for example, from a usage error (invalid flags), invalid rules (also a regex in
a `--rules` file that does not compile, with or without `--no-connect`), an unreadable
`--config` file, a problem in a config file, a `pins.json` that cannot be read or saved (see [Pins
errors](#pins-errors)), a report
that cannot be written (a closed stdout), an unknown home or working directory in auto-discovery,
an `--llm` problem (a missing or invalid `MCPMOAT_LLM_API_KEY`, a provider failure, a provider
refusal of every tool, the 10-minute time limit of the LLM step, an internal error of the LLM
step, or tools over the 500-tool cap), an internal error of the tool rule step, or another
internal error. One tool that the provider refuses (HTTP 400, 413 or 422) is not an execution
error: it is a `medium` finding, and the scan goes on (see [Optional LLM classification](llm.md)).
That is below the default `--fail-on high`, so a hostile server that makes the provider refuse its
tool descriptions can keep their LLM rating from reaching `high`. Some of these errors still print
the report on stdout first, so you can read the findings:
| Execution error | Report |
| A problem in a config file | Printed, then the problems. A `--config` file with a problem and no server prints only the problem. |
| A `pins.json` that cannot be read or saved | Printed |
| An internal error of the inspection (`inspect.Run`) | Printed |
| An LLM provider failure, a provider refusal of every tool, the 10-minute time limit of the LLM step, an internal error of the LLM step, or tools over the 500-tool cap with `--llm` | Printed |
| A signal before the save of new pins | Printed |
| A usage error (also a bad `--llm-*` flag or a missing API key), invalid rules, or an unknown home or working directory | Not printed |
| A signal during the inspection, the tool rule step or the LLM step | Not printed |
| An internal error of the tool rule step. `scan` prints `mcpmoat scan: server <name>: the rule analysis failed (internal error)` | Not printed |
| A report that cannot be written | Not printed |
A signal is Ctrl-C, `SIGTERM` or `SIGHUP`. It gives exit code 2 at these times:
- While `scan` reads the configs. The read stops, and the file it did not read is a config file
problem with the reason `canceled`. If `scan` found a server and you did not use `--no-connect`,
it then stops at the inspection, as in the next item: it prints the line below and no report.
A `pins.json` that cannot be read is the exception: `scan` reads it before the inspection, so
it prints the report and the `pins.json` error, without the line below.
- During the inspection. `scan` stops the stdio servers that it started, prints
`mcpmoat scan: interrupted; no pins were saved`, saves nothing and prints no report.
- During the tool rule step, which applies the description and schema rules to the tools after
the inspection. `scan` stops the rule analysis, prints the same line, saves nothing and prints no
report.
- During the LLM step of a `--llm` scan. `scan` stops the requests and then does the same: it
prints the same line, saves nothing and prints no report. The 10-minute time limit of the LLM
step is not a signal: it prints the report (see the table above).
- After the report, before the save of new pins. `scan` prints the same line and saves nothing.
This applies only when the scan has new servers to pin.
At other times the scan ends with exit code 0 or 1, as if no signal came. A second signal ends
mcpmoat at once.
To use the exit code in CI or in a git hook, see [Using mcpmoat in CI and git hooks](ci.md).
## Pins errors
`scan` and `pin --accept` exit with code 2 when they cannot read or update `pins.json`. With
`scan`, the report is still printed. The causes are:
- The pins directory, a parent directory of it, or `pins.json` is unsafe: another user owns it,
group or others can write it, a macOS ACL lets a user or group write the pins directory or
`pins.json`, or `pins.json` is a symlink, or another user owns a symlink on the path to the pins
directory. A parent passes the owner check when root owns it (group or other write without the
sticky bit is still refused), and a parent with the sticky bit (as `/tmp`) passes the write
check. The error names the path and gives a fix (see [Pins and rug pulls](pins.md)).
- On macOS, an ACL entry of a parent directory of the pins directory lets a user or group change
it: an allow entry with a write right, for any user or group. A deny entry passes, so the default
`everyone deny delete` entry of a home directory is fine. The error names the directory and the
index of the entry, and the fix removes only that entry: `chmod -a# <index> <path>` (or "ask root
to run" it, or "ask the owner or root to run" it, when you do not own the directory).
`ls -led <path>` shows the entries.
- No part of the pins path exists, or a part of it is a file.
- The lock file `pins.json.lock` in the pins directory is unsafe: it is not a regular file (a
symlink, for example), another user owns it, its group or others have any access (mode 0600
passes, 0644 is refused), or on macOS an ACL entry lets a user or group open it. mcpmoat never
changes the mode of an existing lock file. The fix is `rm -- '<path>', then mcpmoat makes a new
one with mode 0600` (`rmdir -- '<path>', ...` when the lock entry is a directory). For an ACL

const (
// maxLineRunes is the longest text, in runes, that one rendered line holds
// after its prefix or indentation. A longer line is wrapped into chunks.
// The report cuts each diff line at a far larger length, so without
// wrapping a payload at the end of one long line would not show in the diff.
maxLineRunes = 200
// maxIndent is the most indentation that a rendered line keeps, in bytes.
// A deeply nested JSON line would else start with so many spaces that the
// report cuts the line before its text, and its change would not show.
maxIndent = 200
// contMarker ends the lead of a wrapped chunk after the first one (see
// render). No real line has it at that place.
contMarker = "+ "
// renderedTool is the shape of the canonical form that render reads. The
// schemas, _meta, icons and the annotations stay raw JSON, because render only
// re-indents them. The field names are the keys that Canonical writes.
type renderedTool struct {
Name         string          `json:"name"`
Title        string          `json:"title"`
Description  string          `json:"description"`
Annotations  json.RawMessage `json:"annotations"`
Meta         json.RawMessage `json:"_meta"`
Icons        json.RawMessage `json:"icons"`
InputSchema  json.RawMessage `json:"inputSchema"`
OutputSchema json.RawMessage `json:"outputSchema"`
// render turns the canonical form of a tool (the output of Canonical, one line
// of JCS) into text with one item per line, so that a line diff is useful.
// Each line of the text is one of these:
//	name: <line of the name>
//	title: <line of the title>
//	description: <line of the description>
//	annotations:
//	  <line of the indented JSON>
//	_meta:
//	  <line of the indented JSON>
//	icons:
//	  <line of the indented JSON>
//	inputSchema:
//	  <line of the indented JSON>
//	outputSchema:
//	  <line of the indented JSON>
// A name, a title or a description with line breaks gives one line for each of
// its lines, and each line has the prefix. So text from a server cannot make
// a line that looks like another field.
// A line with more than maxLineRunes runes after its prefix or indentation is
// wrapped: it becomes several lines of at most maxLineRunes runes, cut on rune
// boundaries. So a line diff shows the chunk that changed, also in a very long
// line. The first chunk keeps the prefix, or the indentation, of the line. The
// next chunks have a continuation lead: the field name and "+ " (for example
// "description+ "), or the indentation and "+ ". A real line never starts like
// that (a field line has ": ", and a JSON line never starts with "+"), so a
// wrapped line and a line break in the text never render the same.
// The JSON parts have two spaces of indent for each level, and the key order
// of the canonical form. A schema, _meta or icons value that the server did not
// send is null.
// mask, when it is not nil, hides secret values (see CompareMasked). render
// applies it to the decoded text before it wraps the lines: to the name, the
// title and the description, and to every string (object keys included) and
// every number in the JSON parts (see maskJSON). So a secret that would be
// split over two wrapped lines is still found. A secret that the server writes
// with a JSON escape (such as \" or \u0041) is also found, because the decode
// removes the escape. The mask does not find a configured value that holds a
// backslash sequence as plain characters (such as the \t and \n of the Windows
// path C:\tools\new_dir) when the server sends the real characters (a tab, a
// newline). The output then escapes those characters, so the value can show.
// docs/limits.md lists this limit. A nil mask changes nothing.
// Apart from the mask, render keeps every byte of the strings as the server
// sent them. It does not escape or normalise anything, so an added invisible
// character is a changed line. The caller must escape the text before it
// writes it to a terminal. render returns an error, and never panics, when
// canonical is not the canonical form of a tool.
func render(canonical string, mask func(string) string) (string, error) {
var t renderedTool
if err := json.Unmarshal([]byte(canonical), &t); err != nil {
// The error of encoding/json can quote input, so it is not wrapped,
// like the error of json.Indent below. The caller adds the context.
return "", errors.New("parse canonical form")
if mask != nil {
if err := maskTool(&t, mask); err != nil {
return "", err
var b strings.Builder
writePrefixed(&b, "name: ", t.Name)
writePrefixed(&b, "title: ", t.Title)
writePrefixed(&b, "description: ", t.Description)
// annotations, _meta and icons come before the schemas, so a large unchanged
// schema cannot push a change in them out of a cut diff. The server controls
// the size of _meta, so a large _meta change, or a large _meta or icons
// value in a new tool, can still push the schemas out (issue #162).
sections := []struct {
label string
raw   json.RawMessage
{"annotations:", t.Annotations},
{"_meta:", t.Meta},
{"icons:", t.Icons},
{"inputSchema:", t.InputSchema},
{"outputSchema:", t.OutputSchema},
for _, s := range sections {
if err := writeIndented(&b, s.label, s.raw); err != nil {
return "", err
return b.String(), nil
// maskTool applies mask to the text fields of t and to the strings and
// numbers of its JSON parts. mask must not be nil. The error names only the
// part, never server text.
func maskTool(t *renderedTool, mask func(string) string) error {
t.Name = mask(t.Name)
t.Title = mask(t.Title)
t.Description = mask(t.Description)
// A pointer to each field lets one loop change the field in place.
parts := []struct {
label string
raw   *json.RawMessage
{"annotations", &t.Annotations},
{"_meta", &t.Meta},
{"icons", &t.Icons},
{"inputSchema", &t.InputSchema},
{"outputSchema", &t.OutputSchema},
for _, p := range parts {
masked, err := maskJSON(*p.raw, mask)
if err != nil {
return fmt.Errorf("mask %s: %w", p.label, err)

import (
"cmp"
"fmt"
"slices"
"github.com/Ducarv/mcpmoat/internal/discover"
"github.com/Ducarv/mcpmoat/internal/report"
"github.com/Ducarv/mcpmoat/internal/rules"
// configRowsPerServer is the largest number of config finding rows that scan
// keeps for one server (issue #213). The config checks add one finding for
// each env key and each header key of a server (MOAT-T4-* and MOAT-T5-*), so a
// hostile project .mcp.json with many short keys could make a huge report. A
// server with more rows gets one summary finding (rules.RuleConfigFindingCap)
// in place of the rest. The step keeps the most severe rows (see
// cutConfigHits), so a server cannot push a severe finding out of the report
// with many weak ones.
const configRowsPerServer = 100
// configRowsTotal is the largest number of config finding rows that scan keeps
// for all the servers together. Without it, a hostile config with many
// servers could still make a huge report, 100 rows at a time. Scan keeps the
// most severe rows of the whole scan, not the rows of the first servers, so
// many servers with weak findings cannot push a severe finding of a later
// server out of the report. A server that loses rows to this cap gets the
// same summary finding as for the per-server cap. That finding does not count
// toward the cap, so the report holds at most configRowsTotal rows plus one
// summary row for each server that lost rows (see docs/limits.md).
const configRowsTotal = 10_000
// configCaps holds the two limits of the config finding rows. A value of zero
// or less means the default (configRowsPerServer and configRowsTotal), so the
// zero configCaps gives the real limits. Tests set small values, so that they
// do not need a hundred findings.
type configCaps struct {
// perServer is the largest number of config rows of one server.
perServer int
// total is the largest number of config rows of the whole scan.
total int
// orDefault returns c with each value of zero or less set to its default.
func (c configCaps) orDefault() configCaps {
if c.perServer <= 0 {
c.perServer = configRowsPerServer
if c.total <= 0 {
c.total = configRowsTotal
return c
// The fixed texts of a rules.RuleConfigFindingCap row (see configCapRow). Like
// the tool findings cap, this rule has no YAML file, so the rule set does not
// hold its texts. They never hold config text.
const (
configCapTitle = "Config findings over the limit are not listed"
configCapRisk  = "This server has more config findings than the report lists, " +
"so the report is short but not complete. A hostile config file can use this to hide a finding among many."
configCapRemediation = "Do not use this server until you have read its config entry yourself: " +
"the command, the args, the URL and the env and header keys. " +
"Treat the findings that the report lists as a sample, not as the full list."
// configChecks holds what the config rules need: the rule set (for the
// severity of a finding), the typosquat check (T5) and the row caps.
type configChecks struct {
set  *rules.Set
typo *rules.Typosquat
// caps holds the limits of the config rows. The zero value gives the
// default limits (see configCaps).
caps configCaps
// configHit is a config finding that the ignore list keeps, while findings
// waits to know which ones fit under the caps. It holds the index of the
// finding in a list, not a copy of it or of its row, so a server with very
// many findings does not hold a row for each one. The memory before the cut is
// not bounded by the caps: findings holds all the findings of one server while
// it cuts them, and then up to the per-server cap for each server until the row
// build (see docs/limits.md).
type configHit struct {
// index is the index of the finding in the list that is cut: the
// findings of one server for the per-server cap, or the hits of all the
// servers for the scan cap.
index int
// severity is the severity word of the row (see findingRule).
severity string
// untrusted is true when the server of the hit comes from a project file
// (discover.Server.Untrusted). The scan cap keeps the hits of other
// servers first among hits of the same severity (see cutConfigHits).
untrusted bool
// configServerHits holds what findings knows about one server after the
// per-server cap, while it waits for the scan cap.
type configServerHits struct {
// ref is the server of the rows. Its Name is the server name, also for
// the ignore key of the cap row.
ref report.ServerRef
// kept holds the findings that the per-server cap keeps, in their first
// order. There are at most caps.perServer of them.
kept []rules.Finding
// start is the index of the first kept finding in the hits of all the
// servers (see findings).
start int
// omitted is the number of findings that the per-server cap left out.
omitted int
// worst is the severity of the cap row for these omitted findings (see
// configCapSeverity). It is high when the per-server cap left out
// nothing.
worst rules.Severity
// findings runs the static config checks on every server and returns one
// report row for each finding that the ignore list does not drop, up to the
// caps. The order of the rows follows the order of servers. For one server,
// the T4 checks (rules.CheckConfig) come first, then the T5 check
// (typo.Check), then the rules.RuleConfigFindingCap row when there is one.
// The servers are checked as discover gives them, with no expansion of
// variables in the command, args or URL. The checks look at the text in the
// config file, not at what a shell would run. Disabled servers are checked
// too, because a user can turn a disabled server on later.
// The severity, the title, the risk and the remediation of a row come from the
// rule set. A finding whose rule is not in the set gets severity "critical"
// (an unknown rule must never pass silently) and empty texts. The report
// leaves out an empty title and prints "-" for an empty risk or remediation.
// A row holds the names of the server and the rule text from the built-in rule
// set (rule ID, field, key, related). It never holds a Finding.Message or a
// config value.
// A server keeps at most cc.caps.perServer rows (configRowsPerServer by
// default), and the whole scan at most cc.caps.total rows (configRowsTotal by
// default). The caps count the rows after the ignore list: a row that the list
// drops does not count, so the user can make room for the other rows. The cut
// has two steps, and each keeps the most severe rows (see cutConfigHits):
//  1. The per-server cap cuts the rows of each server.
//  2. When the rows that are left are more than the scan cap, the scan keeps
//     the most severe of them across all the servers. Among rows of the same
//     severity, it keeps the rows of servers from a user file before the rows
//     of servers from a project file (discover.Server.Untrusted), then the
//     rows of the first servers, and in one server the first rows.
// The kept rows of a server stay in their first order. A server that lost
// rows in one or both steps gets one rules.RuleConfigFindingCap row after its
// kept rows (see configCapRow). It counts all the rows that the server lost
// in the two steps, and its severity is the highest of them, but never lower
// than high. Its limit is the per-server cap when only that cap cut the
// server, and the scan cap when the scan cap cut one or more rows of the
// server. The cap row does not count toward the caps. Below the caps, the
// rows are the same as with no caps. The per-server cut comes first, so the
// scan step holds at most cc.caps.perServer findings for each server.
// Each finding and the cap row go through ignore.ignored. So .mcpmoat-ignore
// can drop a config finding but not the cap row: only --ignore can (see
// fileCannotIgnore). A nil ignore ignores nothing.
// ignored counts the findings that the ignore list dropped, by rule ID. It is
// nil when the list dropped nothing. The caller must tell the user
// about these findings, because an ignore file can come from an untrusted
// folder and hide a finding. The map holds only rule IDs and counts.
// perServer holds, for each server, the number of rows that the server got,
// with the cap row. The index is the index in servers, so two servers with the
// same name are counted apart.
// fileBlocked lists the rule IDs that have a .mcpmoat-ignore entry that
// matches a row but is not applied (see scanIgnores.ignored). It is sorted,
// each ID is in it once, and it is nil when there is no such entry. The caller
// must call warnFileCannotIgnore for each ID.
// cutServers is the number of servers that lost rows to a cap. A server
// counts even when the ignore list then drops its cap row, so the caller can
// still tell the user that the report is not complete.
package report

"fmt"

// emptyCell is what the report prints for a field with no text.
const emptyCell = "-"
// Caps on the rule text of a finding, in runes of raw text. A rule is a YAML
// file in rules/ and its text is one sentence, so a real rule is far below
// these caps. They stop a rule file with a huge text from flooding the screen.
const (
maxTitleRunes    = 200
maxRuleTextRunes = 500
// The severity words of a finding.
const (
severityCritical = "critical"
severityHigh     = "high"
severityMedium   = "medium"
severityLow      = "low"
// severityOrder lists the severity words in the order of the groups of
// WriteFindings: the worst first. A row with any other severity word goes to
// the first group, "critical" (fail closed, like findingRule in
// cmd/mcpmoat). It is an array, not a slice, so no code can change it.
var severityOrder = [...]string{severityCritical, severityHigh, severityMedium, severityLow}
// groupSeverity returns s when it is a known severity word, and "critical"
// otherwise. An unknown severity fails closed: it is grouped and coloured as
// the worst one.
func groupSeverity(s string) string {
if slices.Contains(severityOrder[:], s) {
return s
return severityCritical
// ServerRef names one server and says which config it comes from. Two servers
// can have the same name in two clients or two scopes, so the name alone does
// not tell them apart. FindingRow and ServerStatus embed ServerRef, and both
// print it as "name (client, scope)".
// All strings come from untrusted config files. The report escapes and cuts
// them.
type ServerRef struct {
// Name is the server name in the config.
Name string
// Client is the client whose config declared the server.
Client discover.Client
// Scope is discover.ScopeGlobal or discover.ScopeProject.
Scope discover.Scope
// ProjectPath is the project path of a server with project scope. It is
// empty for a global server.
ProjectPath string
// Untrusted is true for a server from a project file, which a cloned
// repository can ship (discover.Server.Untrusted).
Untrusted bool
// Index is the position of the server in the scanned list. It becomes
// server_index in scan --json, so a JSON consumer can find the server even
// when two names are the same after the cut. The terminal report does not
// print it.
Index int
// NewServerRef returns the ServerRef of s. index is the position of s in the
// scanned list (see ServerRef.Index).
func NewServerRef(s discover.Server, index int) ServerRef {
return ServerRef{
Name:        s.Name,
Client:      s.Client,
Scope:       s.Scope,
ProjectPath: s.ProjectPath,
Untrusted:   s.Untrusted,
Index:       index,
// label returns the escaped text "name (client, scope)". The scope is the
// SCOPE cell of WriteServers: "global", or "project:" and the path, and then
// " (untrusted)" for an untrusted server. Name and client are cut at
// MaxShortCellRunes and the path at maxPathRunes, so a hostile config cannot
// flood the screen.
func (r ServerRef) label() string {
return findingCell(r.Name) + " (" + findingCell(string(r.Client)) + ", " +
scopeCell(r.Scope, r.ProjectPath, r.Untrusted) + ")"
// Source tells what made a finding. It is the type of FindingRow.Source.
type Source string
// The values of FindingRow.Source. The zero value "" means SourceRule.
const (
// SourceRule is a finding from a mcpmoat rule (a built-in check or a rule
// file), not from the LLM.
SourceRule Source = "rule"
// SourceLLM is a finding from the optional LLM classification (--llm). It
// is advisory: a model made it, not a rule.
SourceLLM Source = "llm"
// normalize returns the source that the writers use for s: SourceLLM stays

// FindingRow is one finding as the report prints it. It holds names and the
// text of the rule, never a value from a config. The caller fills Severity,
// Title, Risk and Remediation from the rule set, because this package does not
// know the rules.
type FindingRow struct {
// ServerRef is the server that the finding is about.
ServerRef
// Source tells what made the finding. The zero value means SourceRule.
// WriteFindings marks a SourceLLM row as advisory.
Source Source
// RuleID is the ID of the rule that matched.
RuleID string
// Severity is the severity word of the rule: "critical", "high", "medium"
// or "low". Any other word is shown in the group "critical".
Severity string
// Title is the short title of the rule. WriteFindings leaves it out when
// it is empty.
Title string
// Risk says why the finding matters. It is the text of the rule.
Risk string
// Remediation says how to fix the finding. It is the text of the rule.
Remediation string
// Field is the config field that matched, for example "env" or "args". A
// pin row has the field "tool" and the tool name in Key.
Field string
// Key is the key name in Field, for example an env variable name.
Key string
